1380.title: A God who suffers
1380.hook: the cross says God is not distant from pain
1380.howItsDone: Christians meditate on the cross in times of suffering, through crucifixes, icons of the crucifixion, Good Friday services and the Stations of the Cross, and some pray with Christ's own cry from Psalm 22.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in the dark. Your line was even darkness can be prayed.

"Jesus wept." In the King James Bible, that's a whole verse, two words long. He's on his way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, at the village of Bethany. Mary, Lazarus's sister, has just fallen at his feet, crying. So are the people with her. John says Jesus groaned in the spirit and was troubled, and then he weeps. The strange part: In the story, he's about to call Lazarus out of that tomb. He knows how this ends. He weeps anyway.

Christians believe Jesus is God come in the flesh. So when he weeps at Bethany, they see more than a sad friend. They see God crying at a funeral. He doesn't give Mary a lecture on death. He weeps with her. Next, Isaiah, whose suffering servant you met back in year two: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." Acquainted with grief: not a visitor to it, a neighbor. Jewish readers read the passage differently, some as speaking of the people of Israel; Christians hear Christ in it. Then the cross. On the cross, Mark says, darkness came over the whole land, and Jesus cried out the opening of another psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Some Christians say this is close to the heart of their answer to suffering, such as it is: not an explanation, but God inside the pain. Theologians put this carefully, and differently. Some say God's own nature cannot suffer, and that Christ suffered in his human nature, truly, as one person. Others speak more boldly of the suffering of God. Churches hold these with care. Both point to one picture: on the cross, God is not watching from far off. Last, Hebrews: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." Christ knows weakness from the inside. Not above the pain, explaining. In it. If grief has you feeling in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

Choose someone you've never met, a name in the news, a stranger in a waiting room, a worn face you passed today, and picture them where they are. If you pray, picture God not above them but beside them, in the chair by the bed, weeping with them the way Jesus wept at Bethany, and say their name to God, nothing else; if you don't, simply picture them not alone.
A God who suffers. The Christian belief that in Jesus, God weeps at a grave and goes to the cross: not distant from pain.
Your line: god in the pain. Not watching from far off, but close. See you tomorrow.

1381.title: Compassion
1381.howItsDone: Christians practice compassion by visiting the sick and grieving, bringing meals, sitting with the dying and giving to those in need; churches organize care teams, hospital chaplaincies and works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a God who suffers: Jesus weeping near the tomb of his friend. Your line was god in the pain.

A funeral is coming out through the gate of a town called Nain. A young man is being carried out on a bier. Luke gives the detail that makes it unbearable: he was "the only son of his mother, and she was a widow." A crowd from the town walks with her. Coming up the road the other way is Jesus, with his own crowd. Two processions meet at the gate. Nobody asks him for anything. Luke says that when he saw her, something moved in him before he said a word or lifted a hand.
screen: `A FUNERAL AT THE GATE OF NAIN.`

segments.voice: Some readers hear two Latin pieces inside the English word compassion: with, and suffering. Suffer with: not pity handed down, but feeling it from beside. The Gospels' word goes lower still: "And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not." The Greek verb is splanchnizomai, and some readers hear in it the gut: being moved in your insides. You met that gut-deep word back on day one hundred eighty-three, with a crowd like sheep without a shepherd. Luke uses it of the Samaritan who stops for the man left half dead on the Jericho road: "he had compassion on him." And of the father in the parable of the lost son: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Notice the order. The feeling comes first, then the body moves. Jesus touches the bier, and the young man sits up. The Samaritan goes to him and binds up his wounds. The father runs. Compassion here isn't a mood; it ends in the hands and feet. Last, Paul makes it a job for ordinary people: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." And: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." Some Christians link it to yesterday: if God suffers with people, following him means doing the same. It doesn't answer why there is suffering. It answers a different question: what now?

Choose someone hurting whom you could actually reach, and picture the conversation: notice the pull to keep it short, to cheer them up, to fix it, and picture yourself staying instead, listening longer than is comfortable, letting a silence sit. If you pray, you can bring them to God; if you don't, let the picture of staying be enough for now. And if they ever say they're in danger, in the US you can call or text 988 together, or reach local emergency help.
Compassion. Suffering with someone: being moved inside, and then staying close.
Your line: suffer with. Feeling first, then the hands. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.

1382.title: Illness
1382.hook: praying, seeking medicine, and trusting are not opposites
1382.howItsDone: Christians pray for the sick, by name in services and privately, while also seeking medical care; some churches anoint the sick with oil, following the letter of James, and Catholic and Orthodox churches keep this as a sacrament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion: suffering with someone, not fixing them from a distance. Your line was suffer with.

A hospital waiting room. A woman holds a rosary in one hand and a list of her husband's medications in the other. Across from her, a man reads the side effects on a pill bottle, then closes his eyes for a moment, lips moving. Nobody in that room thinks they have to choose. Yet the question comes up in some families: if you really trusted God, would you need the doctor? And if you go to the doctor, were the prayers just for show? Some ordinary Bible verses speak to it.

You first heard this at Levi's table. When critics asked why Jesus ate with sinners, he answered: "They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick." He used doctors as his picture of help that's needed, not a lack of faith. The letter of James tells the sick to call the elders of the church: "let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." King Hezekiah, sick to the point of death, hears through Isaiah: "I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears." Then the prophet calls for something from the kitchen: "Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaster upon the boil." Prayer heard, and a poultice on the sore. Paul tells his young friend Timothy, in the King James words, "use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities." Practical advice, in the middle of scripture. And to the Colossians he names a companion: "Luke, the beloved physician." Tradition holds that this same Luke wrote one of the Gospels. A doctor, counted among the friends of the church. Now what this doesn't promise. Christians who pray for healing don't all mean the same thing by it. Some expect dramatic recoveries and pray boldly for them. Others pray mostly for strength, peace and good doctors. Some churches anoint the sick as a sacrament; others lay on hands, or simply pray. What the texts keep doing is holding prayer and care together. Hands that pray, and hands that bandage.
screen: `A PRAYER HEARD, A POULTICE OF FIGS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing in your body that needs care right now: a pill you take, a sore back, a checkup you've been putting off, a night of sleep you keep skipping. Hold it without judging yourself, and if you pray, name it to God, the way the sick in James are told to. Then choose one plain, practical step for it, and hold the two side by side.
Illness. A weakness of the body that the Bible meets with prayer and with practical care, a physician and an anointing, held together.
Your line: both, not either. A pill and a prayer can share a morning. That's today, done.

1383.title: When faith and depression meet
1383.hook: depression isn't a lack of faith; saints and preachers have known it, and help is good
1383.howItsDone: Some Christians who live with depression combine prayer, scripture and church community with counseling, medical care and medication, and some churches and pastors speak openly about mental health and encourage people to seek professional help.

segments.voice: Yesterday, illness: elders who pray and anoint, and Luke, the beloved physician. Your line was both, not either.

A prophet has just had an enormous day. Fire from heaven, a crowd face down on the ground. Then one message arrives from the queen, a threat on his life, and he runs. A day's journey into the wilderness, alone, he sits down under a juniper tree. And there, the text says, he asks to die. "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life." This is Elijah. Not a beginner. Not someone short on faith. A man who has just seen God answer by fire, lying under a bush, done.

Notice first what God does not do. There's no lecture under that tree. Elijah falls asleep, and an angel touches him and says, "Arise and eat." Bread baked on coals, a jar of water. He eats, and sleeps again. The angel comes back: "Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee." Sleep, food, and someone who comes back. Some readers hear in this something close to what we'd now call depression, and notice how bodily the care is. The talking comes later. The psalms give words for it. Psalm forty-two keeps asking: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me?" A person of prayer, talking to their own heavy soul, still reaching for hope, still not feeling it. The Bible leaves that question in the prayer book. Others have known this from the inside. The London preacher Charles Spurgeon, in his lectures to students for the ministry, wrote openly about his own crushing low seasons, which came on him even while he kept preaching. In stories like his, a dark season says nothing, by itself, about how strong someone's faith is. Last, help. Yesterday's lesson said prayer and medicine belong together, and that holds for the mind as much as the body. Counselors, doctors, medication, a friend who keeps coming back like that angel. Some pastors put it plainly: getting help is part of being cared for by God, not a failure of it.
screen: `ARISE AND EAT: SLEEP, FOOD, A RETURN.`
`WHY ART THOU CAST DOWN, O MY SOUL?`

segments.voice: If you're carrying a heaviness right now, think of one person you could tell: a friend, a doctor, a counselor, a pastor; if you're doing all right, think of someone who's gone quiet lately. Just choose the name, and if you pray, bring that name to God. If you're in danger right now, stop and contact emergency services or a crisis line where you live, or call or text 988 in the US; that comes first.
When faith and depression meet. Elijah under the tree, the psalm's cast-down soul: a darkness the Bible meets with food, sleep, honest prayer, and help.

1384.title: Grief
1384.hook: Jesus wept; grief is love continuing
1384.howItsDone: Christians mourn through funerals, wakes and shared meals; Catholics pray and offer Masses for the dead, Orthodox Christians hold memorial services, and churches name the dead in prayer, holding sorrow and the hope of resurrection together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, when faith and depression meet: Elijah under the juniper tree, and an angel saying arise and eat. Your line was seek help, it's holy.

"Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Martha says it on the road outside Bethany, the moment Jesus arrives. Her brother Lazarus has been in the tomb for days. Later her sister Mary comes out, falls at his feet, and says the very same words. Two sisters, one sentence. If only you had been here. Grieving people still say some version of it, to God, to a doctor, to themselves. And in John's telling, Jesus doesn't correct either of them.

That sentence is half complaint, half trust: you could have stopped this, and you didn't come. John lets both sisters say it out loud, and nobody scolds them. Martha keeps talking, and the two of them talk on the road about death and rising again. Grief, in this chapter, is allowed to speak. Then come the two words that make a whole verse in the King James Bible: Jesus wept. When the mourners see it, they say, "Behold how he loved him!" Not how weak he is. How he loved him. Some do ask why he couldn't have prevented the death, but the first thing John records is love. That's today's line: grief is love continuing after the person is gone. Paul, writing to grieving Christians in Thessalonica, wants them to "sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." He doesn't tell them not to sorrow. He talks about how: with hope alongside. Some Christians hear that as comfort; some hear it, on hard days, as a weight. Both are honest. And in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says, "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." The mourners are the ones named blessed. Churches carry it differently: funerals and wakes, Orthodox memorial services with candles and a sweet dish of wheat, Catholics praying for the dead by name, Protestant families gathering for a meal after the burial. Different customs, one instinct: grief deserves room.

Bring to mind someone or something you've lost, a person, a place, a version of your life, and let one memory come: their voice, a kitchen, a phrase they used. If tears come, let them; if nothing comes, that's all right too; if you pray, tell God their name, and if you don't, hold the memory a little longer than you usually let yourself. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Grief. The sorrow of loss, which Jesus himself wept, and which the crowd at Lazarus's tomb read as love.
Your line: grief is love. At Bethany, even the tears were read that way. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1385.title: Doubt
1385.hook: doubt is not unbelief; Thomas doubted and was still an apostle
1385.howItsDone: Christians remember Thomas on his feast day and read his story in church on the Sunday after Easter in some traditions; some churches hold groups where questions and doubts are spoken aloud, and the father's prayer from Mark is prayed as a short prayer of its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grief: Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, and the crowd said, behold how he loved him. Your line was grief is love.

Thomas missed the meeting. On the evening the tomb is found empty, the disciples are behind locked doors, and the risen Jesus stands among them. Thomas isn't there. When he gets back, the others are almost shouting: we have seen the Lord. And Thomas says no. "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." For a whole week he's the one in the room who can't say yes.

You met Thomas in year one; today, a closer look. After eight days the doors are shut again, and this time Thomas is there. Jesus goes straight to him. No scolding speech. He offers exactly what Thomas asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing." The doubter gets a visit of his own. Then what Thomas says. The text never says he touched the wounds. He answers, "My Lord and my God." The man remembered for doubting calls Jesus, plainly, both Lord and God. The doubt didn't disqualify him; it was the road he took to get there. And he isn't alone. At the end of Matthew's Gospel, the disciples meet Jesus on a mountain: "they worshipped him: but some doubted." Worship and doubt in one sentence, one crowd, and Jesus sends all of them out anyway. In Mark, a desperate father brings his son to Jesus and cries out, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both in one breath, and Jesus heals the boy. Last, where Thomas went. Tradition says he traveled east, as far as India, and some Christians in India keep that story as their own. The doubter, in that telling, became a messenger to a far country. So some Christians draw a line here. Unbelief walks away. Doubt stays in the room and asks to see.
screen: `TRADITION SAYS: ALL THE WAY TO INDIA.`

segments.voice: Let one honest question come up, about God, about faith, about a story you've heard, or about yourself, and name it in one plain sentence, the way Thomas did: here's what I can't say yes to yet. Don't argue with it or rush to answer it; breathe beside it, the way you'd sit beside a friend who's unsure. If you pray, you can borrow the father's words: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
Doubt. An honest question that stays in the room. Thomas doubted, was visited, and spoke the words my Lord and my God.
Your line: doubt belongs. Thomas was visited, not sent away. See you in the morning.

1386.title: A saint's long darkness
1386.hook: Mother Teresa's letters revealed decades without feeling God's presence, yet she kept going
1386.howItsDone: Catholics honor Mother Teresa as Saint Teresa of Calcutta, and her Missionaries of Charity keep a daily rhythm of prayer and service to the poor; some Christians of other churches read her letters too as encouragement to keep praying through seasons when God feels absent.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Thomas asked to see the nails, and Jesus came back for him. Your line was doubt belongs.

A small woman in a white sari with blue stripes, bending over a dying man on a mat. Cameras followed her for years. She founded houses for the poor and the dying, spoke to presidents, and smiled in the photographs. Catholics now call her Saint Teresa of Calcutta. After she died, her private letters to her spiritual directors were published. And in them, page after page, she describes darkness. Emptiness. A God she couldn't feel. Prayer that seemed to go nowhere. All the while, she kept getting up to pray, and going back to the mats.

You met her in year three; this is what she kept hidden. She wrote of longing for God and not feeling him at all. Of a place in her soul that felt empty. Of smiling on the outside while the inside felt like night. These were letters to the priests guiding her, and some she had hoped would stay private. She kept going. The prayer, the chapel, the work with the sick, without the feeling that once carried her. Her directors helped her see the darkness not as proof that God had left, but as part of following a Christ who himself cried out on the cross. In her sisters' chapels, as their tradition keeps it, words of Jesus from the cross in John's Gospel are written beside the crucifix: "I thirst." The Bible has room for this. Isaiah speaks to the one "that walketh in darkness, and hath no light," and says, "let him trust in the name of the LORD." Trust while it's dark. Paul writes, "For we walk by faith, not by sight." And the prophet Habakkuk sings of a time when the fig tree doesn't blossom and the fields yield nothing: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD." In spite of how it feels. Some Christians assume that if God feels far away, something has gone wrong with their faith. Her letters suggest another picture: faith can be a decision you keep making with your feet, when your feelings have gone quiet.

Think of one thing you've kept doing after it stopped feeling meaningful: a prayer, a visit, a promise, caring for someone. Just notice that you're still doing it, and let that count. If you pray, pray as usual, even if nothing seems to come back; if you don't, simply stay with the breath. If the dark ever turns into thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
A saint's long darkness. Mother Teresa's hidden years of feeling no presence of God, kept company by prayer and work that never stopped.
Your line: faith without feeling. The week ran from a God who suffers to a saint in the dark. That's the week.
